source: Written for Wayword as a learner's guide; not part of the original dataset. Examples are dataset phrases.
intro: Most Arabic letters map onto English sounds. These are the ones that don't, plus a few Levantine habits. Spoken Levantine differs from formal Arabic, and this guide follows the city speech the dataset uses.
reading: CAPITALS mark the stressed syllable: MAR-ha-ba.
Doubled vowels (aa, ee, oo) are long. Hold them.
In this dataset a capital H often marks the throaty ح (bteH-KEE, mneeH), but not always: ha-LEEB and HAM-maam are ح too.
An apostrophe or a vowel standing alone often marks ع: t'eed, ba-EED, A-ra-bee.

sounds.name: Ḥa
sounds.how: A strong, breathy h pushed from a tightened throat, like fogging up glasses with force. It is smooth, with no scrape or gargle.

sounds.name: ʿAyn
sounds.how: A squeeze deep in the throat with the voice on. Tighten the muscles you'd use to gag, then say "ah". As a beginner, a short catch in the voice is close enough to be understood.

sounds.name: Kha
sounds.how: Like the ch in Scottish "loch" or German "Bach": air scraping at the back of the mouth.

sounds.name: Ghayn
sounds.how: The voiced partner of خ, close to a French r: a soft gargle with the voice on.

sounds.name: Qaf
sounds.how: In city Levantine (Amman, Jerusalem, Beirut, Damascus) ق usually becomes a glottal stop, the catch in the middle of "uh-oh". Rural Palestinians and many Jordanians say a hard g instead, and formal Arabic uses a deep k. The dataset uses the city catch.

sounds.name: Heavy letters
sounds.how: Heavy versions of s, d, t and z. Pull your tongue back and lower it so the sound comes out deeper. That also darkens nearby vowels toward "ah" and "aw". Using a plain s or t is understood, but sounds foreign.

sounds.name: Jim
sounds.how: Palestinians and Jordanians mostly say j as in "jam". In Lebanon and Syria you'll often hear zh, as in "measure". Both are fine.

sounds.name: Doubled letters
sounds.how: A doubled consonant is held for longer: linger on it before moving on. Shortening it can turn it into a different word.

sounds.name: Hamza (catch)
sounds.how: A quick stop in the throat, like the break in "uh-oh". The Levantine "no" (لأ) ends with one, which makes it sound clipped and firm.
